study.title: They have not prevailed against me
study.intro: Psalm 129 is the testimony of a people who have been attacked again and again since their youth, yet are still standing. Israel speaks like one person with a scarred back, plowed over by cruel enemies, but set free by the righteous LORD. The psalm then prays that those who hate Zion will wither like grass on a rooftop, never growing into a harvest.
study.context: Israel's 'youth' points back to slavery in Egypt (Hosea 11:1) and continues through the attacks of Philistines, Assyrians and Babylonians. This Song of Ascents uses the same call as Psalm 124: 'let Israel now declare.' Flat clay rooftops in Israel often sprouted thin grass after rain that quickly dried up in the sun. The closing verse refers to the customary greeting exchanged between harvesters and passersby (Ruth 2:4).
study.peopleNote: No author is named. Israel speaks as one person who has suffered long persecution. The enemies are those who hate Zion. God is never portrayed as a human figure in planned art.

verses.title: Attacked from youth
verses.heading: Many a time they have persecuted me
verses.meaning: 'Many a time they have persecuted me from my youth—let Israel now declare—' Israel looks back over its whole history and sees a long line of attacks, beginning in Egypt when the nation was young. The people are invited to say it together, owning their story. Remembering past suffering honestly is not self-pity; it sets the stage for remembering how God has kept them through it all.
verses.context: Hosea 11:1 speaks of Israel as a child God called out of Egypt. Exodus 1:11-14 describes the harsh slavery there. Psalm 124:1 uses the same invitation, 'let Israel now declare,' to retell God's faithfulness.
explore: Persecuted
Attacked, pressed hard or oppressed, especially because of who someone is or whom they belong to.
From my youth
From the earliest days; for Israel, from the time of slavery in Egypt.
verses.reflect: What hardships have marked your story from early on? Can you also see where God kept you?
verses.alt: Ancient stone ruins on a hillside with new grass growing between them.

verses.title: Not overcome
verses.heading: They have not prevailed against me
verses.meaning: 'many a time they have persecuted me from my youth, but they have not prevailed against me.' The line repeats, but this time with a powerful 'but.' The enemies attacked many times, yet they did not win. God's people have often been knocked down but never knocked out. This is the testimony of faith in every generation: the battles were real, but the outcome was decided by God.
verses.context: Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 4:8-9 that believers are hard pressed but not crushed, struck down but not destroyed. Jesus promised in Matthew 16:18 that the gates of Hades will not prevail against His church.
explore: Prevailed
Won, gained the victory, or overpowered someone completely.
But
A turning word that changes the direction of a sentence from loss to hope.
verses.reflect: Where can you say, 'They attacked me, but they did not win'?
verses.alt: A weathered olive tree still standing on a windswept ridge.

verses.title: Furrows on my back
verses.heading: The plowmen plowed over my back
verses.meaning: 'The plowmen plowed over my back; they made their furrows long.' This is one of the most painful pictures in the Psalms. Israel's suffering is compared to a field being plowed, the enemies cutting long grooves across the nation's back like a whip leaves stripes. It speaks of deep, lasting wounds. The honesty of this verse shows that God does not ask His people to pretend their pain is small.
verses.context: Isaiah 51:23 describes oppressors who said, 'Lie down so we can walk over you,' making Israel's back like the ground. Isaiah 50:6 speaks of offering one's back to those who strike. Jesus was flogged before His crucifixion (John 19:1).
explore: Plowmen
Farmers who drive a plow through the soil to break it up and cut grooves for planting.
Furrows
Long, narrow trenches cut into the ground by a plow.
verses.reflect: What wounds have you carried for a long time? Can you name them honestly before God?
verses.alt: Long plowed furrows stretching across a field at dusk.

verses.title: Cut free by the Righteous One
verses.heading: He has cut me from the cords
verses.meaning: 'The LORD is righteous; He has cut me from the cords of the wicked.' Here is the turn. The plowing imagery continues: oxen were tied to the plow with ropes. God simply cut the cords, and the plowing stopped. He did it because He is righteous, just and faithful to His people. Our freedom does not depend on our strength, but on the character of the God who will not let wickedness run forever.
verses.context: Oxen were harnessed to plows with cords and yokes. Leviticus 26:13 says God broke the bars of Israel's yoke so they could walk upright. Psalm 116:16 says, 'You have loosed my bonds.'
explore: Righteous
Always doing what is right and just; God's perfect moral goodness.
Cords
Ropes used to harness oxen to a plow or to tie someone up.
verses.reflect: What 'cords' do you need God to cut in your life right now?
verses.alt: A cut rope lying beside an abandoned plow in a field.

verses.title: Turned back in shame
verses.heading: May all who hate Zion
verses.meaning: 'May all who hate Zion be turned back in shame.' The psalm now prays about the enemies. It does not ask for revenge in its own hands, but for those who hate God's people and God's city to be stopped and turned back. Their plans should fail and be exposed. This is a prayer that evil would not win, handed over to God rather than carried out by the one praying.
verses.context: Psalm 35:4 prays that those who plot harm be turned back in disgrace. Romans 12:19 tells believers not to take revenge but to leave room for God's wrath. Zion stands for God's people and His dwelling.
explore: Zion
Jerusalem, the city of God's temple, standing for God's people and His presence.
Shame
Disgrace that comes when wrong plans fail and are exposed.
verses.reflect: How can you pray honestly about people who oppose God's work without taking revenge yourself?
verses.alt: Riders turning back from a city gate on a dusty road.

verses.title: Grass on the rooftop
verses.heading: Withers before it can grow
verses.meaning: 'May they be like grass on the rooftops, which withers before it can grow,' Flat roofs of clay and earth in Israel often sprouted thin grass after a rain. It looked green for a moment, but with no deep soil it quickly dried up in the sun. The psalm prays that the enemies' power be like that: showy for a moment, but with no roots and no future.
verses.context: Houses had flat roofs of packed earth where grass could sprout briefly. 2 Kings 19:26 describes nations as grass on the housetops, scorched before it grows. Jesus' parable of the sower describes seed on rocky ground that withers for lack of root (Mark 4:5-6).
explore: Rooftops
Flat roofs made of beams, branches and packed clay, used for drying and sleeping.
Withers
Dries up, shrivels and dies, like plants without enough water or soil.
verses.reflect: What looks impressive now but has no real roots? How does this verse change your view of it?
verses.alt: Thin dry grass sprouting on a flat clay rooftop under hot sun.

verses.title: No harvest to gather
verses.heading: Unable to fill the hands of the reaper
verses.meaning: 'unable to fill the hands of the reaper, or the arms of the binder of sheaves.' Rooftop grass never becomes a harvest. A reaper could not even get a handful, and there would be nothing to bind into sheaves. The enemies' efforts will ultimately produce nothing that lasts. In contrast, God's people, plowed and wounded, will bear fruit, as Psalm 126 promised a harvest of joy.
verses.context: Reapers cut grain with sickles, and binders tied it into sheaves. Psalm 126:6 promised returning with sheaves of grain. Galatians 6:8 says whoever sows to the flesh will reap destruction.
explore: Reaper
A harvester who cuts ripe standing grain with a hand sickle at harvest time.
Binder of sheaves
A worker who gathers cut grain stalks into bundles and ties them together.
verses.reflect: What are you investing in that will produce a real, lasting harvest?
verses.alt: A reaper with an empty hand standing in a barren patch of field.

verses.title: No blessing spoken
verses.heading: The blessing of the LORD be on you
verses.meaning: 'May none who pass by say to them, “The blessing of the LORD be on you; we bless you in the name of the LORD.”' At harvest, passersby would greet workers with a blessing, and the workers would answer back. But the enemies of Zion will have no harvest and so no greeting. The psalm ends quietly, with silence where blessing should be. Those who oppose God's people cut themselves off from the blessing God loves to give.
verses.context: Ruth 2:4 records Boaz greeting the harvesters, 'The LORD be with you,' and their reply, 'The LORD bless you.' Genesis 12:3 promises blessing to those who bless Abraham's people, and loss to those who curse them.
explore: Passersby
People walking past on the road who would greet workers in a field.
In the name of the LORD
By God's authority and character, invoking His presence and favor.
verses.reflect: Whom can you speak a blessing over today, the way harvesters greeted each other?
verses.alt: Harvesters in a golden field raising hands in greeting to a passing traveler.
